stem_md: A rectangular building consists of  $30$  square rooms situated like the cells of a  $2 \times 15$  board. In each room there are three doors, each of which leads to another room (not necessarily different). How many ways are there to distribute the doors between the rooms so that it is possible to get from any room to any other one without leaving the building?
solution_md:
In a  $2$ x $N$  building let the rows be labelled  $A$  and  $B$ , and the columns labelled  $1, 2, ..., N$ . We denote cells  $X$  and  $Y$  having exactly one door in common by  $X-Y$ , exactly two doors in common by  $X- - Y$  and exactly three doors in common by  $X- - - Y$  and exactly no doors in common by  $XY$ .
Let the function  $f(N)$  denote the number of possible arrangements of doors (3 per room and all accessible to each other) in a  $2$ x $N$ .

Let  $g(N)$  denote the number of ways to finish of a building of size  $N+1$ , with connections:  $A1- - B1$ , and  $A1-A2$  and  $B1-B2$ . Suppose  $N>2$ , now suppose  $A2-B2$ , then  $A2- A3$  and  $B2-B3$ , this leads to  $g(N-1)$  possibilities. On the other hand if  $A2B2$ , then  $A2- - A3$  and  $B2- - B3$ , now  $A3$  and  $B3$  can't have connections as that would cut of the rest of the building below, therefore  $A3B3$ , so  $A3-A4$  and  $B3-B4$ , which leaves  $g(N-2)$  possibilities. Therefore  $g(N)=g(N-1)+g(N-2)$  for  $N>2$ . Note: it is easy to check no other connections for  $A2$  and  $B2$  work. Also it is easy to check that  $g(1)=1$  and  $g(2)=2$ , so  $g(N) = F_{N-1}$ , where  $F_n$  is the nth Fibonacci number  $(F_1=F_2=1)$ Now for  $f(N)$  suppose  $N > 2$ , if  $A1- - B1$  then  $A1-A2$  and  $B1-B2$  which leaves  $g(N-1)$  possibilities. If  $A1-B1$ , then  $A1- - A2$  and  $B1- - B2$ , then  $A2$  and  $B2$  are can not be connected otherwise the rest of the building is disconnected, so  $A2B2$ , then  $A2-A3$  and  $B2-B3$  and we are left with  $g(N-2)$  possibilities. It is easy to check no other connections for  $A1$  and  $B1$  work. So  $f(N) = g(N-1)+g(N-2) = g(N)$ . So  $f(15) = 987$ .

stem_md:
The vertices of a regular  $n + 1$ -gon are denoted by  $P_0,P_1,...,P_n$  in some order ( $n \ge 2$ ). Each side of the polygon is assigned a natural number as follows: if the endpoints of the side are  $P_i$  and  $P_j$ , then the assigned number equals  $|i - j |$ . Let S be the sum of all  $n + 1$  assigned numbers.
(a) Given  $n$ , what is the smallest possible value of  $S$ ?
(b) If  $P_0$  is fixed, how many different assignments are there for which  $S$  attains the smallest value?
solution_md:
Start at  $P_0$ , and move clockwise summing the absolute differences. Eventually we get to  $P_n$  and so we would have summed at least  $n$ . Then we eventually get back to  $P_0$ , which adds at least another  $n$  to the total. Therefore  $S \ge 2n$ , and it is clear this is possible by ordering them:  $P_0, P_1, ..., P_n$ .

Clearly  $S=2n$  if and only if from  $P_0$  to  $P_n$  it is strictly increasing (clockwise and anticlockwise) (because if it isn't then it will have  $S=2n+\epsilon$ ,  $\epsilon>0$  by similar argument to the above). This is clearly equal to the number of ways we can construct an ordered bipartition of  ${P_1, P_2, ..., P_{n-1}}$ , which is  $2^{n-1}$ .

stem_md:
A function  $f: R \to R$  satisfies the conditions:  $f (x + 19) \le f (x) + 19$  and  $f (x + 94) \ge f (x) + 94$  for all  $x \in R$ .
Prove that  $f (x + 1) = f (x) + 1$  for all  $x \in R$ .
solution_md:
Observe that 
\[
f(x+95)\le f(x+76)+19\le f(x+3\cdot 19)+2\cdot 19\le \cdots \le f(x) + 95,
\]
by iterating the first identity. Now that  $f(x+95)=f(x+1+94)\ge f(x+1)+94$ , it follows that  $f(x)+1\ge f(x+1)$ . Now, if there is an  $x$  such that  $f(x)+1>f(x+1)$ , then we get
\[
f(x)+94>f(x+94)\ge f(x)+94,
\]
a contradiction. Hence,  $f(x+1)=f(x)+1$  for all  $x$ .

stem_md: Given real numbers  $a, b$ , find all functions  $f: R \to R$  satisfying $f(x,y) = af (x,z) + bf(y,z)$  for all  $x,y,z \in R$ .
solution_md:
$\textrm{Ans:}$  
\[f(x,y)=\begin{cases} \textrm{const.} \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \textrm{if  $a+b=1$  and  $(a,b)\ne(1,0)$ }  \textrm{any function of  $x$ } \ \ \ \ \ \ \textrm{if  $(a,b)=(1,0)$ } 0 \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \  \textrm{if ( $a=1$  and  $b\ne -1,0$ ) or ( $a+b\ne 1$  and  $a\ne 1$ )}  f(x)-f(y)  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \textrm{if  $(a,b)=(1,-1)$ } \end{cases}\]
It is easy to see that the above function satisfies the FE. We now show that it is the only solution. Let  $P(x,y,z)$  denote the given assertion, we have  $P(0,0,0) \implies f(0,0)=(a+b)f(0,0)$ . Now, we split into cases:  $\line(1,0){600}$  $\textbf{\color{red}{Case 1:}}$   $a+b=1$ . 
We have \[P(x,x,y) \implies f(x,y)=f(x,x).\] Then,  $bf(x,x)=(1-a)f(x,x)=f(x,y)-af(x,z)=bf(y,z)$ . 
If  $b\ne 0$ , we get  $f(x,y)=f(x,x)=f(y,z)$  and we can see that  $f\equiv \textrm{const.}$  
If  $(a,b)=(1,0)$ , we have  $f(x,x)=f(x,y)=f(x,z)$  and so  $f$  can be any function of  $x$ .  $\line(1,0){600}$  $\textbf{\color{red}{Case 2:}}$   $a+b\ne1$ .
Since  $f(0,0)=0$ , we have \[P(x,0,0) \implies f(x,0)=af(x,0).\] If  $a\ne 1$ , we get  $f(x,0)=0$  and by using this, \[P(x,y,0) \implies f(x,y)=0.\] If  $a=1$ , by  $P(0,0,x)$ , this gives  $f(0,x)+bf(0,x)=0$ . 
Now, if  $b\ne -1$ , then  $f(0,x)=0$  and using  $P(0,x,y)$ , we have  $bf(x,y)=0$ . 
Note that since  $b\ne 0$  (as  $a+b\ne 1$ ), we have  $f(x,y)=0$  in this case. 
Next, if  $b=-1$ , \[P(x,0,y) \implies f(x,y)=f(x,0)+f(0,y).\] Also,  $P(x,y,z)$  and  $P(y,x,z)$  yields  $f(x,y)=-f(y,x)$  which means  $f(x,0)=-f(0,x)$ . Therefore,  $f(x,y)=f(x,0)-f(y,0)$ . In this case, we can see that  $f(x,y)=f(x)-f(y)$  for any function  $f$ .
And WE ARE DONE!  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Let  $n > 1$  be an odd positive integer. Assume that positive integers  $x_1, x_2,..., x_n \ge 0$  satisfy:  $$ \begin{cases} (x_2 - x_1)^2 + 2(x_2 +x_1) + 1 = n^2 
(x_3 -x_2)^2 + 2(x_3 +x_2) + 1 = n^2 
...
(x_1 - x_n)^2 + 2(x_1 + x_n)+ 1 = n^2 \end {cases} $$  Show that there exists  $j, 1 \le j \le n$ , such that  $x_j = x_{j+1}$ . Here  $x_{n+1} = x_1$ .
solution_md:
Using the quadratic formula on any of the equation gives  $x_{i+1}=x_i-1 \pm \sqrt{n^2-4x_i}$   $(*)$ Let  $n=2k+1$ , we know that  $n^2-4x_i$  is a square. So that give us that  $x_i=(k+t+1)(k-t)$  for some  $-k-1\le t \le k$ . Let  $a_t = (k+t+1)(k-t)$ .
Suppose  $x_i = a_j$ , using  $(*)$  gives  $x_{i+1}=a_{j-1}$  or,  $a_{j+1}$ , this is obtained after basic algebraic manipulation and some factoring. It is also easy to check,  $a_t=a_{-t-1}$ .
Let the pairs containing equal values:  $(a_0, a_{-1}), (a_1, a_{-2}), ..., (a_k, a_{-k-1})$  each be denoted as a stage.

Moving from  $x_1$  to  $x_1$  again (by going cyclically around  ${x_1, ..., x_n}$ ), we must start and end on the same stage, and n is odd therefore if each time we are going up or down a stage then the sequence  ${x_i}$  can not be formed, as we can't get back to the starting stage in an odd number of moves. Therefore at some point we must move to a successive term in the  ${x_i}$  sequence without changing stage (note we can't move more than 1 stage at a time). The only way to accomplish this is to move from one term in the stage  $(a_0, a_{-1})$  to the other. But they are equal in value and thus this proves the desired result.

stem_md: The sequences  $(a_n)$  and (c_n) are given by  $a_0 =\frac12$ ,   $c_0=4$  , and for  $n \ge 0$  ,  $a_{n+1}=\frac{2a_n}{1+a_n^2}$ ,  $c_{n+1}=c_n^2-2c_n+2$ Prove that for all  $n\ge 1$ ,   $a_n=\frac{2c_0c_1...c_{n-1}}{c_n}$
solution_md:
Sweet.

Note that  $c_{n+1}-1= (c_n-1)^2$ .  Letting  $d_n\triangleq c_n$ , we have  $d_0=3$  and  $d_{n+1}=d_n^2$ , for   $n\geqslant 0$ . Consequently,   $d_n=3^{2^n}$ , and  $c_n=3^{2^n}+1$  for every  $n\geqslant 0$ . With this, we conclude that  $$ \frac{2c_0c_1\cdots c_{n-1}}{c_n} = \frac{3^{2^n}-1}{3^{2^n}+1}. $$  Note that,  $$ a_n = \frac{2c_0c_1\cdots c_{n-1}}{c_n}  \Leftrightarrow \frac{1+a_n}{1-a_n} = 3^{2^n}.  $$  We now prove the last claim. Note that,  $$ 1+a_{n+1}=\frac{(a_n+1)^2}{1+a_n^2}\quad\text{and}\quad 1-a_{n+1}=\frac{(1-a_n)^2}{1+a_n^2}. $$  Consequently,   $$ \frac{1+a_{n+1}}{1-a_{n+1}} = \frac{1+a_n}{1-a_n}. $$  Since  $(1+a_0)/(1-a_0)=3$ ,  we have the desired claim.

stem_md: Solve in integers the following equation $\frac{1}{2}(x + y)(y + z)(z + x) + (x + y + z)^3 = 1 - xyz$ .
solution_md: Let  $x+y+z=c$ , so  $\frac{1}{2}(c-x)(c-y)(c-z) + c^3 = 1-xyz$ . This simplifies to $xyz+xyc+xzc+yzc-xc^2-yc^2-zc^2+3c^3=2$ , and using  $x+y+z=c$ , we get $xyz+xyc+xzc+yzc+xc^2+yc^2+zc^2+c^3=2$ , which factors into $(x+c)(y+c)(z+c)=2$ , so we can simply consider all triplets of integers that multiply to 2. Ignoring permutations, this simplifies to 3 cases. It is just simple linear systems of equations so I won't show it. But 1 of the cases leads to non-integer solutions and the other two cases gives: $(x,y,z)=(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1),  (2, -1, -1),  (-1, 2, -1),  (-1, -1, 2)$

stem_md: Determine all polynomials  $P(x)$  with real coefficients such that $P(x)^2 + P\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)^2=  P(x^2)P\left(\frac{1}{x^2}\right)$  for all  $x$ .
solution_md:
Clearly  $P\equiv 0$  works. We show there are no other solutions. Clearly  $P$  is non-constant. Taking  $x=1$  we get  $P(1)=0$ , thus  $P(x)=(x-1)^n Q(x)$  for some  $Q\in\mathbb{R}[x]$  where  $Q(1)\ne 0$ . Plugging this in we get
\[
Q(x)^2 + \frac{1}{x^{2n}}Q\left(\frac1x\right)^2 = (-1)^n \frac{(x+1)^{2n}}{x^{2n}}Q(x^2)Q\left(\frac{1}{x^2}\right).
\]
Taking  $x=1$  once again and recalling  $Q(1)\ne 0$ , we have  $2=(-1)^n 2^{2n}$ , a contradiction. Thus  $Q\equiv 0$  and  $P\equiv 0$ .

solution_md: I claim  $a_i=0$ ,  $1\le i\le n$ , is the only solution. Suppose the contrary and observe that we have  $\textstyle \sum_{i\le n}a_i=0$  by summing  $n$  equalities. Now, let  $k$  be such that  $\textstyle a_k = \max_{1\le i\le n}a_i$ . Note that if there is a solution other than  $(0,0,\dots,0)$  then  $a_k>0$ . The equation  $a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}$  then implies  $a_{k-1},a_{k-2}\ge 0$  (where the arithmetic on indices is modulo  $n$ ). Now we use  $a_{k+1} = a_k+a_{k-1}$ . If  $a_{k-1}>0$ , we have  $a_{k+1}>a_k$ , a contradiction. Thus  $a_{k-1}=0$  and  $a_{k+1}=a_k$ . But now,  $a_{k+2}=a_{k+1}+a_k=2a_k>a_k$  as  $a_k>0$ , contradicting with the maximality of  $a_k$ .

stem_md: A sphere  $S$  divides every edge of a convex polyhedron  $P$  into three equal parts. Show that there exists a sphere tangent to all the edges of  $P$ .
solution_md: Let  $O$  be the center of  $S$ . For any adjacent vertices  $X, Y$  of  $P$  denote  $S \cap XY=X_1, Y_1$ . For all edges  $XY$  of  $P$   $O$  lies on the perpendicular bisector plane of  $X_1Y_1$  which coincides with that of  $XY$ . It follows that  $O$  is equidistant from all vertices of  $P$ . Then note that in all the isosceles triangles  $OXY$  with equal edges  $OX=OY$  the base  $XY$  is trisected by the endpoints of the equal segments  $OX_1=OY_1$ . This is possible only if all this isosceles triangles  $OXY$  are equal. Hence the distance of  $O$  from any edge is equal to the altitudes of the equal triangles  $OXY$  drawn to base and there exists a sphere centered at  $O$  that is tangent to all the edges of  $P$ .

stem_md:
Real numbers  $x,y,z, t$  satisfy  $x + y + z +t = 0$  and  $x^2+ y^2+ z^2+t^2 = 1$ . 

Prove that  $- 1 \le xy + yz + zt + tx \le 0$ .
solution_md: We have \[0\ge -(x+z)^2 =(x+z)(y+t)=xt+yz+zt+tx.\] Then since  $0=(x+y+z+t)^2=1+2(xy+xz+xt+yz+yt+zt), xy+tx+yz+zt=\frac{-1}{2}-xz-yt$ , it is suffices to prove that  $xz+yt\le \frac{1}{2}$  which is true by AM-GM, \[xz+yt \le \frac{x^2+z^2}{2}+\frac{y^2+t^2}{2}=\frac{1}{2}. \blacksquare\]

stem_md: Show that there is no integer-valued function on the integers such that  $f(m+f(n))=f(m)-n$  for all  $m,n$ .
solution_md:
Suppose there was. 

Let  $P(m,n)$  denote the assertion.  $P(m,f(m)): f(m+f(f(m))) = 0$ . 

If  $f(c) = 0$ , then  $P(m,c): f(m) = f(m) - c$ , so  $c=0$ . 

Thus  $m+f(f(m)) = 0$  for all  $m$ , which implies  $f(f(m)) = -m$ . 

Claim:  $f$  is bijective. 
Proof: To show surjective, note that  $f(m) -n$  can take any integer value. 

If  $f(a) = f(b)$ , then  $P(m,a)$  and  $P(m,b)$  gives that  $a=b$ .  $\square$  $P(-f(m),m): f(-f(m)) = m$ . 

Since  $f(f(m))= -f(-f(m))$ , we have  $f$  is odd.  $P(m,f(-n)): f(m+n) = f(m) + f(n)$ . So  $f$  is additive and over the integers, which implies  $f(x) = kx$  for some  $k$ . 

Then  $f(f(m)) = -m$ , so  $k^2  = -1$ , contradiction.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/Austrian-Polish/1997 Austrian-Polish Competition/566112.json

stem_md:
Find all pairs of real numbers  $(x, y)$  satisfying the following system of
equations $2-x^{3}=y, 2-y^{3}=x$ .
solution_md:
If  $x=y$  then we must have  $x=y=1$ , so assume  $x\ne y$ . We have  $(x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2) = (x-y)$  and thus  $x^2+xy+y^2=1$ . Likewise, we have  $4=x^3+y^3+x+y = (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2+1) = 2(x+y)(x^2+y^2)$ . Setting  $a=x+y$ , we then have  $x^2+y^2=2/a$ . Moreover,
\[
2=2x^2+2xy+2y^2 = (x+y)^2 +x^2+y^2 = a^2 + \frac2a \implies a^3-2a+2=0.
\]
It is not hard to see that if  $a^3-2a+2=0$  ( $a\in\mathbb{R}$ ) then  $a<0$ . This, however, is a contradiction:  $x^2+y^2=2/a<0$ . Hence, no solutions unless  $x=y$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/Austrian-Polish/1998 Austrian-Polish Competition/112861.json

candidates: The function  $f(t)=2-t^{3}$  is decreasing on whole  $\mathbb{R}$ , hence  $f(x)=y\land f(y)=x\implies f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$  can have solution iff  $f(x)=x$ , giving  $x^{3}+x-2=0\iff (x-1)(x^{2}+x+2)=0$ . The only real solution is  $x=1\implies y=1$

If  $R$  denotes the circumradius and  $r$  the inradius of the triangle, show that  $r+KX+LY+MZ=2R$ .
solution_md:
Let  $O$  be the circumcentre of the triangle. [Carnot's Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnot%27s_theorem_(inradius,_circumradius)) tells us:
\[r+R=OK+OL+OM\]
Add  $2R$  and subtract  $OK$ ,  $OL$  and  $OM$  from both sides to get:
\[r+3R-(OK+OL+OM)=2R\]
And note that  $R-OK=KX$ , and similarly for the others, to get the desired:
\[r+KX+LY+MZ=2R\]

stem_md: Determine all pairs  $(a, b)$  of positive integers for which the equation  $x^3 - 17x^2 + ax - b^2 = 0$  has three integer roots (not necessarily different).
solution_md:
Hi, i'm new here, and sorry for reviving this topic, but this is such a nice problem.

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>First of all, let  $r_1,r_2,r_3\in \displaystyle \mathbb {Z}$  be the roots of  $f(x)=x^3-17x^2+ax-b^2=0$ . Notice that all roots must be positive. Otherwise, let's say WLOG that  $r_1<0$ , then  $f(r_1)<0$ , because each term of  $f(x)$  is negative (remember  $m,n\in\displaystyle \mathbb {Z}^*_+$ ), but that's absurd. Now, we have:   $$ r_1+r_2+r_1=17 $$    $$ r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1= m $$    $$ r_1r_2r_3=n^2 $$  It is easy to see that if a prime number greater or equal to  $11$  divides  $n$ , then  $r_1+r_2+r_3>17$ , and this reduces the problem a lot already. If  $7\mid n$ , then necessarily 7 divides exactly two of the roots (let's say  $r_1$  and  $r_2$ ), but that implies  $r_3=3$  and  $n^2=7^2\cdot 3$ , which is not possible. If  $5\mid n$ , it is easy to see that  $10+5+2=17$  and  $10\cdot 5 \cdot 2=100=10^2$ , so this works. If 5 is not a divisor of  $n$ , we only have to check the cases where  $2\mid n$  and/or  $3\mid n$ . Being careful, we find out that  $(10,5,2),(4,4,9),(8,1,8),(8,6,3)$  are the only possible values for the roots of  $f(x)$ . This leads to  $(n,m)=(10,80),(12,88),(8,80),(12,90)$  by the previous equations.</details>

stem_md: In each unit square of an infinite square grid a natural number is written. The polygons of area  $n$  with sides going along the gridlines are called *admissible*, where  $n > 2$  is a given natural number. The *value* of an admissible polygon is defined as the sum of the numbers inside it. Prove that if the values of any two congruent admissible polygons are equal, then all the numbers written in the unit squares of the grid are equal. (We recall that a symmetric image of polygon  $P$  is congruent to  $P$ .)
solution_md:
Superimpose the grid onto the coordinate plane such that the axes lie on grid lines. 

We consider two cases:**<u>*$n$  is odd.*</u>** 
Let  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  be two adjacent unit squares, and let  $e$  be their common edge. Let  $T$  be an  $n-1$  by 1 rectangle adjacent to both  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  and symmetric about  $e .$  Then  $s_{1} \cup T$  and  $s_{2} \cup T$  are two congruent admissible polygons, so if they have the same value, then the values in  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  are the same. It follows that all of the numbers written in the squares are equal.**<u>*$n$  is even*</u>**
Let  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  be two squares separated by exactly one square  $s$ . Suppose that  $s_{1}$  and  $s$  share the common edge  $a ; s_{2}$  and  $s$  share the common edge  $b$ ; and that  $a \| b$ . Let  $T$  be an  $n-1$  by 1 rectangle adjacent to both  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  and symmetric with respect to  $s .$  Then  $s_{1} \cup T$  and  $s_{2} \cup T$  are two congruent admissible polygons, so if they have the same value, then the values in  $s_{1}$  and  $s_{2}$  are the same. Thus, if we color the grid like a chess board, all the white squares share a common value  $x$  and all the black squares share a common value  $y$ .

Now consider the following two admissible polygons. The first is defined by a row of  $n-2$  unit squares with one unit square added to each side, at one end. (This looks like a  $T$ -shape, with a very short top of- $T$  and a very long bottom-of- $T$ .) The second is obtained by translating the first polygon by the vector  $[0,1] .$  One of the polygons has value  $\frac{(n-2)(x+y)}{2}+2 x$ , and the other has value  $\frac{(n-2)(x+y)}{2}+2 y$  Thus  $x=y$  and we are done.

stem_md: For positive integers  $m, n$ , denote   $$ S_m(n)=\sum_{1\le k \le n} \left[ \sqrt[k^2]{k^m}\right] $$  Prove that  $S_m(n) \le n + m  (\sqrt[4]{2^m}-1)$
solution_md:
First, assume  $k\ge m+1$ . In this case, using  $2^k>k$ , we havve
\[
2^{k^2}>k^k>k^m \implies 2>\sqrt[k^2]{k^m}> 1.
\]
Hence, 
\[
\left[\sqrt[k^2]{k^m}\right] = 1,\quad \text{for}\quad m+1\le k\le n.
\]
Hence, it suffices to show 
\[
\sum_{1\le k\le m}\left[\sqrt[k^2]{k^m}\right]\le m2^{\frac{m}{4}}.
\]
Finally, we have 
\[
2^{k^2}\ge k^4 \implies 2^{\frac{m}{4}}\ge k^{\frac{k^2}{m}},
\]
thus the claimed inequality is indeed true.

stem_md: For n points \[ P_1;P_2;...;P_n \] in that order on a straight line. We colored each point by 1 in 5 white, red, green, blue, and purple. A coloring is called acceptable if two consecutive points \[ P_i;P_{i+1} (i=1;2;...n-1) \] is the same color or 2 points with at least one of 2 points are colored white. How many ways acceptable color?
solution_md:
Let's try to clean up the language:

A line of  $n$  points is given.  The points are to be colored using the five colors white, red, greed, blue and purple such that for each pair of consecutive points, either both are the same color or at least one of the points is white.  In how many ways can this be done?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Well, this is a natural question for a recursive approach (e.g., as in [http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=410085](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=410085)).  Let  $a_n$  be the number of colorings whose last point is colored white, and let  $b_n$  be the number of colorings in which the last point is colored anything other than white.  Thus  $a_0 = 1$ ,  $b_0 = 0$ , and for  $n \geq 1$  we have  $a_n = a_{n - 1} + b_{n - 1}$  and  $b_n = (k - 1)a_{n - 1} + b_{n - 1}$ .  Now we solve to eliminate  $b$ : substituting from the first equation into the second, I get  $a_{n + 1} - a_n = 4a_{n - 1} + (a_n - a_{n - 1})$ , whence  $a_{n + 1} = 2a_n + 3a_{n - 1}$ .  It follows from standard techniques that  $a_n = A \cdot 3^n + B \cdot (-1)^n$ ; putting in the initial values  $a_0 = a_1 = 1$  we have  $A = B = \frac{1}{2}$ .  Thus  $a_n = \frac{3^{n} + (-1)^n}{2}$ .  The total number of colorings is  $a_n + b_n = a_{n + 1} = \boxed{\frac{3^{n + 1} + (-1)^{n + 1}}{2}}$ .</details>

stem_md:
A sequence of integers  $(a_n)$  satisfies  $a_{n+1} = a_n^3 + 1999$  for  $n = 1,2,....$  
Prove that there exists at most one  $n$  for which  $a_n$  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
If  $a_n = k^2 (k\geq 0)$ , when  $a_n \in \{0,1,4\}(mod$   $8).$ 1)  $a_n \in \{0,4\}(mod$   $8)\implies a_{n+1} \in \{-1, -2\} (mod$   $8)\implies\forall m > n: a_{m} \in \{-1, -2\} (mod$   $8)$  $\implies\forall m > n: a_{m}$  isn't a perfect square.
2)  $a_n \equiv 1 (mod$   $8)\implies a_{n+1} \equiv 0 (mod$   $8)\implies a_{n+2} \in \{-1, -2\} (mod$   $8)$  $\implies \forall m > n+1: a_{m} \in \{-1, -2\} (mod$   $8)$   $\implies\forall m > n+1: a_{m}$  isn't a perfect square.
If  $a_{n +1}= y^2 (y\geq 0)$ , when  $1999 = y^2-k^6=(y-k^3)(y+k^3)\implies y- k^3 = 1 $  and  $y+k^3 = 1999$   $\implies k^3 = (1999 - 1 )/2 = 999$  - contradiction.

stem_md: Given an integer  $n \ge 2$ , find all sustems of  $n$  functions $ f_1,..., f_n : R \to R$  such that for all  $x,y \in R$   $$ \begin{cases} f_1(x)-f_2 (x)f_2(y)+ f_1(y) = 0  f_2(x^2)-f_3 (x)f_3(y)+ f_2(y^2) = 0  ...  f_n(x^n)-f_1 (x)f_1(y)+ f_n(y^n) = 0 \end {cases} $$
solution_md:
Inserting  $x=y$  in the first equation gives us that   $$ 2f_1(x)=f_2(x)^2  $$    $$  \implies (f_1(x)+f_1(y))^2= (f_2 (x)f_2(y))^2=4f_1(x)f_1(y) $$    $$ \implies(f_1(x)-f_1(y))^2=0 \implies f_1(x)=f_1(y)  $$     $$ \implies f_1(x)=C \text{ for some constant C}  $$  Since  $f_1$  is constant then in the first equation by setting  $y$  fixed and changing  $x$  ( if  $f(y)=0$  and we assume that  $f_2$  is not constant we can find a  $y_0$  that  $f(y_0) \ne 0$  and we set  $y_0$  instead of  $y$  )we get that  $f_2(x)$  is also constant and the same goes for  $f_3, \dots ,f_n$ .
So all of the functions are constant ,then assume that  $f_i=C_i$  , we see that for all  $1\leq i \leq n$  :  $$  \implies 2C_i=C_{i+1}^2  $$  It is EZ to see that  $\quad C_1^2=2C_n \text{(by the last equation)} \quad \text{and} \quad 2^{2^{i-1}-1} C_1=C_i^{2^{i-1}}\quad$    ,  So inserting  $n$  instead of  $i$  in the later we get that :  $\quad C_1=2 \quad \text{or}\quad  C_1=0$   
If  $C_1=0$  then  $0=C_2=C_3= \dots =C_n$ If  $C_1=2$  then  $2=C_2=C_3= \dots =C_n$  $Q.E.D$

stem_md: For each integer  $n \ge 3$  solve in real numbers the system of equations:  $$ \begin{cases}  x_1^3 = x_2 + x_3 + 1 ...x_{n-1}^3 = x_n+ x_1 + 1x_{n}^3 = x_1+ x_2 + 1 \end{cases} $$
solution_md:
Let  $t$  be any root of  $t^3=2t+1\iff (t+1)(t^2-t-1)=0$ . Then we claim  $x_i=t$ ,  $1\le i\le n$ , is the only solution. 

Let  $x_i=\textstyle \max_{j\le n}x_j$ . Using  $x_i^3\ge x_{i-1}^3$  we find  $x_{i+2}=x_i$ . Repeating this, we find  $x_i=x_{i+2}=x_{i+4}=\cdots$ . Now,  $x_{i-1}^3 = x_i+x_{i+1}+1=x_{i+2}+x_i+1=x_i^3$  yields, together with the monotonicity of  $t\mapsto t^3$ ,  $x_{i-1}=x_i$ . Iterating the idea above, we find all  $x_i$  are in fact equal. Setting  $x_i=t$ , we arrive at  $t^3=2t+1$  yielding  $(t+1)(t^2-t-1)=0$ .

stem_md: For which integers  $n \ge 5$  is it possible to color the vertices of a regular $ n$ -gon using at most  $6$  colors in such a way that any  $5$  consecutive vertices have different colors?
solution_md:
We use casework on the number of vertices  $n$ .

1.  $n$  is of the form  $5x$ : In this case, we will just choose any five of the six colors, and repeat them in that same order.
2.  $n$  is of the form  $5x + 6y$ , where  $y > 0$ : We will choose any five of the six colors, say  $(a, b, c, d, e)$ , repeat them in that same order  $x$  times, and use  $y$  chains of all of the six letters in the same order  $(a, b, c, d, e, f)$ .
3.  $n = 7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 19$  (which are the only numbers that are not represented in the above forms): 
We will show that the coloring is not possible. Let  $n = 6k + l$ , where  $l = 0, .., 5$ . Now since  $n < 6(k + 1)$ , at least  $k + 1$  vertices are of the same color by PHP, which suggests that  $n > 5k + 5$ , which is not true for the above numbers.

Thus our final answer is the given range excluding only the set  ${7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 19}$ .

stem_md: Find all polynomials  $P(x)$  with real coefficients having the following property: There exists a positive integer n such that the equality   $$ \sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}(-1)^k \left[\frac{k}{2}\right] P(x + k)=0 $$  holds for infinitely many real numbers  $x$ .
solution_md:
I claim the only such  $P$  are constant.

Let  $P\equiv c$ . Note that taking  $n=1$ , the given sum is  $P(x+2)-P(x+3)=0$  for all  $x\in\mathbb{R}$ . We now show there are no non-constant  $P$  satisfying the given condition. Assume the contrary, let  ${\rm deg}(P)=d$ . Notice that we can assume  $P$  is monic. We have
\[
\sum_{1\le i\le n}i\bigl(P(x+2i)-P(x+2i+1)\bigr)=0
\]
for infinitely many  $x$ . Checking that the RHS is a polynomial of degree  $d-1$ , it must then be a zero polynomial. Now, the coefficient of the term  $x^{d-1}$  in  $P(x+2i)-P(x+2i+1)$  is  $2id - (2i+1)d=-d$ . Hence, the coefficient of  $x^{d-1}$  for RHS is  $d\textstyle \sum_{1\le i\le n}i$ . This is a clear contradiction as it is a zero polynomial.

stem_md: Find all positive integers  $N$  having only prime divisors  $2,5$  such that  $N+25$  is a perfect square.
solution_md:
$N + 25 = M^2  \Rightarrow   N = M^2 - 25 = (M+5) (M-5)$ .

If  $5 \not{\mid} M$ , then  $M+5$  and  $M-5$  are powers of  $2$ , which is not possible.
Hence  $5 \mid M$ , let  $M = 5K$ . Thus  $N = (5K+5)(5K-5) = 25(K+1)(K-1)$ .

If  $5 \not{\mid} (K+1)(K-1)$ , then  $K+1$  and  $K-1$  are powers of  $2 \Rightarrow K=3 \Rightarrow \boxed{N = 200}$ .
If  $5 \mid (K+1)(K-1)$ , we have two cases:

(a)  $5 \mid K+1 \Rightarrow K-1$  is a power of  $2$ . Since  $K$  is at least  $4$ , we have  $K-1 = 2^{\alpha}$  and  $K+1 = 2 \cdot 5^{\beta}$ , with  $\alpha \geq 2$  and  $\beta > 0$ . Thus  $2 \cdot 5^{\beta} - 2 = 2 (5^{\beta} - 1) = 2^{\alpha}$ . Hence  $5^{\beta} - 1$  is a power of  $2 \Rightarrow \beta = 1 \Rightarrow K = 9 \Rightarrow \boxed{N = 2000}$ . (Notice if  $\beta > 1$  then  $5^{\beta} - 1$  is divisible by  $8$ , so  $\beta$  is even, but then it is also divisible by  $3$ ).

(b)  $5 \mid K-1 \Rightarrow K+1$  is a power of  $2$ . Since  $K$  is at least  $6$ , we have  $K+1 = 2^{\alpha}$  and  $K-1 = 2 \cdot 5^{\beta}$ , with  $\alpha \geq 3$  and  $\beta > 0$ . But this has no solutions: we have  $2 \cdot 5^{\beta} + 2 = 2 (5^{\beta} + 1)$  is a power of  $2$ , but  $2 \parallel 5^{\beta} + 1$ , and  $5^{\beta} + 1 > 2$ .

So the only solutions are  $N = 200, 2000$ .

stem_md:
If three nonnegative reals  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  satisfy  $a+b+c=1$ , prove that
 $2 \leq \left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}\leq \left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)$ .
solution_md:
If three nonnegative reals $a$ , $b$ , $c$ satisfy $a+b+c=1$ , prove that $2 \leq \left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}\leq \left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)$ .
See also http://www.kalva.demon.co.uk/aus-pol/apsol/asol009.html , and there is a weaker version of the left part at http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=27430 . For what it is worth, let me present a different solution: **Left part:** We have to prove that, if a, b, c are nonnegative numbers satisfying a + b + c = 1, then $2\leq\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}$ . Indeed, note that $\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}=\left(\left(1+a\right)\left(1-a\right)\right)^{2}=\left(1+a\right)^{2}\left(1-a\right)^{2}$ . By the Bernoulli inequality, $\left(1+a\right)^{2}\geq 1+2a$ ; thus, since $\left(1-a\right)^{2}\geq 0$ , we get $\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}\geq\left(1+2a\right)\left(1-a\right)^{2}$ . Similarly, $\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}\geq\left(1+2b\right)\left(1-b\right)^{2}$ and $\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}\geq\left(1+2c\right)\left(1-c\right)^{2}$ . But, as you can easily check, the identity $\left(1+2a\right)\left(1-a\right)^{2}+\left(1+2b\right)\left(1-b\right)^{2}+\left(1+2c\right)\left(1-c\right)^{2}-\left(2+6abc\right)$ $=\left(a+b+c-1\right)\left(2a^{2}+2b^{2}+2c^{2}-2bc-2ca-2ab-a-b-c-1\right)$ holds, so that, since a + b + c = 1, we have a + b + c - 1 = 0 and $\left(1+2a\right)\left(1-a\right)^{2}+\left(1+2b\right)\left(1-b\right)^{2}+\left(1+2c\right)\left(1-c\right)^{2}-\left(2+6abc\right)=0$ , and thus $\left(1+2a\right)\left(1-a\right)^{2}+\left(1+2b\right)\left(1-b\right)^{2}+\left(1+2c\right)\left(1-c\right)^{2}=2+6abc\geq 2$ . Hence, $\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}$ $\geq\left(1+2a\right)\left(1-a\right)^{2}+\left(1+2b\right)\left(1-b\right)^{2}+\left(1+2c\right)\left(1-c\right)^{2}\geq 2$ , qed. **Right part:** We have to prove that, if a, b, c are nonnegative numbers satisfying a + b + c = 1, then $\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-b^{2}\right)^{2}+\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{2}\leq\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)$ . Using the cyclic sum notation, this inequality becomes $\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}\leq\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)$ . Now, since a + b + c = 1, we have $\sum\left(1-a\right)=3-\left(a+b+c\right)=3-1=2$ , and thus $2\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}$ $=\sum\left(1-a\right)\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}$ $=\sum\left(\left(1-a\right)\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}\right)$ . But $\left(1-a\right)\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}=\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}$ $=\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\left(1-a^{2}\right)\right)=\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(2a^{2}+bc+b+c-1\right)$ , and, using a + b + c = 1, we have $2a^{2}+bc+b+c-1=2a^{2}+bc+\left(b+c\right)\left(a+b+c\right)-\left(a+b+c\right)^{2}=\left(a-b\right)\left(a-c\right)$ , so that $\left(1-a\right)\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}=\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(a-b\right)\left(a-c\right)$ , and the above becomes $2\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)=\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(a-b\right)\left(a-c\right)$ . Now, note that, since the nonnegative numbers a, b, c sum up to 1, they are all $\leq 1$ , so their squares $a^{2}$ , $b^{2}$ , $c^{2}$ are $\leq 1$ , too, and thus, the numbers $1-a^{2}$ , $1-b^{2}$ , $1-c^{2}$ are all nonnegative. Also, note that we can WLOG set $a\geq b\geq c$ ; then, $a^{2}\geq b^{2}\geq c^{2}$ , so that $1-a^{2}\leq 1-b^{2}\leq 1-c^{2}$ . Thus, we can apply the Vornicu-Schur inequality (Lemma 1 in http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=24555 post #9) with $x=1-a^{2}$ , $y=1-b^{2}$ , $z=1-c^{2}$ , and get $\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)\left(a-b\right)\left(a-c\right)\geq 0$ . Because of the above, this implies $2\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)-2\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)\geq 0$ , so that $\sum\left(1-a^{2}\right)^{2}\leq\left(1+a\right)\left(1+b\right)\left(1+c\right)$ . And the proof is complete. This is probably not the simplest solution, but, at least, it nowhere requires calculating expressions of degree more than 3, so it's better than straightforward bunching ;) . Darij

stem_md: The prism with the regular octagonal base and with all edges of the length equal to  $1$  is given. The points  $M_{1},M_{2},\cdots,M_{10}$  are the midpoints of all the faces of the prism. For the point  $P$  from the inside of the prism denote by  $P_{i}$  the intersection point (not equal to  $M_{i}$ ) of the line  $M_{i}P$  with the surface of the prism. Assume that the point  $P$  is so chosen that all associated with  $P$  points  $P_{i}$  do not belong to any edge of the prism and on each face lies exactly one point  $P_{i}$ . Prove that \[\sum_{i=1}^{10}\frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}=5\]
solution_md:
Let  $B_{1}B_{2}...B_{8}$  and  $T_{1}T_{2}...T_{8}$  be the bottom and top bases of the prism. Let  $M_{1}, M_{2}, ...$  be the midpoints of the faces  $B_{1}B_{2}T_{2}T_{1},\ B_{2}B_{3}T_{3}T_{2}, ...$  etc., and  $M_{9}, M_{10}$  the midpoints of the bottom and top bases. Assume  $M_{9}P$  intersects a face, say  $B_{1}B_{2}T_{1}T_{2}.$   $M_{10}P$  can intersect only the same face, which is not allowed by the problem conditions, or the bottom base. By the 1st condition, P is in the volume  $B_{1}B_{2}T_{2}T_{1}M_{9},$  by the 2nd condition in the volume  $B_{1}B_{2}...B_{8}M_{10}.$  These 2 volumes intersect in the bottom half of the prism, where P must be located, hence neither the ray  $M_{9}P$  nor one of the rays  $M_{1}P, M_{2}P, ... M_{8}P$  intersects the top base, which is contrary to the problem conditions. Thus  $M_{9}P$  must intersect the top base and  $M_{10}P$  the bottom one. Consider the parallel projections (in the vertical direction)  $N_{1}, N_{2}, ..., N_{8}, Q$  of  $M_{1}, M_{2}, ..., M_{8}, P$  to the bottom base. Assume the ray  $N_{1}Q$  intersects the segment  $B_{2}B_{3}.$  Then Q is in the triangle  $\triangle B_{2}B_{3}N_{1}$  and only one of the 6 rays  $N_{3}Q, N_{4}Q, ..., N_{8}Q$  can intersect this triangle. Hence  $N_{1}Q$  cannot intersect  $B_{2}B_{3}.$   Assume the ray  $N_{1}Q$  intersects the segment  $B_{3}B_{4}.$  Then Q is in the triangle  $\triangle B_{3}B_{4}N_{1}$  and only 2 of the 5 rays  $N_{4}Q, N_{5}Q, ..., N_{8}Q$  can intersect this triangle. Hence  $N_{1}Q$  cannot intersect  $B_{3}B_{4}.$   Assume the ray  $N_{1}Q$  intersects the segment  $B_{4}B_{5}.$  Then Q is in the triangle  $\triangle B_{4}B_{5}N_{1}$  and only 3 of the 4 rays  $N_{5}Q, N_{6}Q, ..., N_{8}Q$  can intersect this triangle. Hence  $N_{1}Q$  cannot intersect  $B_{4}B_{5}.$  Similarly,  $N_{1}Q$  cannot intersect the segments  $B_{8}B_{1}, B_{7}B_{8}, B_{6}B_{7},$  so that it must intersect the only remaining segment  $B_{5}B_{6}\parallel B_{1}B_{2}.$  Likewise,  $N_{2}Q$  intersects the opposite parallel segment  $B_{6}B_{7},$   $N_{3}Q$  intersects the opposite parallel segment  $B_{7}B_{8},$  etc. Thus all the rays  $M_{i}P,\ i = 1, 2, ..., 10$  intersect the opposite parallel faces or bases of the prism. It follows that 2 triangles in all 5 triangle pairs  $\triangle M_{i}PP_{k}\sim \triangle P_{i}PM_{k}$  are centrally similar with similarity center P, having parallel sides, so that
 $\frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}= \frac{P_{k}P}{P_{k}M_{k}}$ 
 $\frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}+\frac{M_{k}P}{M_{k}P_{k}}= \frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}+\frac{P_{k}M_{k}-P_{k}P}{P_{k}M_{k}}= \frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}+1-\frac{P_{k}P}{P_{k}M_{k}}= 1$ 
 $\sum_{i = 1}^{10}\frac{M_{i}P}{M_{i}P_{i}}= 5$

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer greater than  $2$ . Solve in nonnegative real numbers the following system of equations \[x_{k}+x_{k+1}=x_{k+2}^{2}\quad , \quad k=1,2,\cdots,n\] where  $x_{n+1}=x_{1}$  and  $x_{n+2}=x_{2}$ .
solution_md:
Summing all equations we get: $ \sum{x_i^2} = \sum{2x_i}$  $ \sum{(x_i-1)^2} = n$ First case: there exists  $a$  such that  $x_a \leqslant 1$  $\Rightarrow x_a^2 = x_{a-1} + x_{a-2} \leqslant 1$  $\Rightarrow x_{a-1} \leqslant 1$  $\Rightarrow (x_i - 1)^2 \leqslant 1$  $\Rightarrow x_i = 0$ Second case: all numbers are greater than one
Let  $a$  be such that  $(x_a - 1)^2$  is maximised  $\Rightarrow x_a$  is maximised $\Rightarrow 2x_a \geqslant x_{a-1} + x_{a-2}$ By Dirichlet Principle:  $(x_a-1)^2 \geqslant 1 \Rightarrow x_a \geqslant 2$  $x_{a-2} + x_{a-1} = x_a^2 \geqslant 2x_a$  $\Rightarrow x_a^2 = 2x_a \Rightarrow x_a = 2$ Obviously follows that all  $x$  must be  $2$ , which is indeed a solution

stem_md: The fields of the  $8\times 8$  chessboard are numbered from  $1$  to  $64$  in the following manner: For  $i=1,2,\cdots,63$  the field numbered by  $i+1$  can be reached from the field numbered by  $i$  by one move of the knight. Let us choose positive real numbers  $x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{64}$ . For each white field numbered by  $i$  define the number  $y_{i}=1+x_{i}^{2}-\sqrt[3]{x_{i-1}^{2}x_{i+1}}$  and for each black field numbered by  $j$  define the number  $y_{j}=1+x_{j}^{2}-\sqrt[3]{x_{j-1}x_{j+1}^{2}}$  where  $x_{0}=x_{64}$  and  $x_{1}=x_{65}$ . Prove that \[\sum_{i=1}^{64}y_{i}\geq 48\]
solution_md:
Note that the  $i$  corresponding to white fields are either the even or odd integers;  WLOG assume it is the even integers.  By the rearrangement inequality, we have
 $\sum_{k=1}^{32}\sqrt[3]{x^{2}_{2k-1}x_{2k+1}}\leq \sum_{k=1}^{32}x_{2k-1}$ 

and similarly, 
 $\sum_{k=1}^{32}\sqrt[3]{x_{2k}x^{2}_{2k+2}}\leq \sum_{k=1}^{32}x_{2k}$ .

So
 $\sum_{i=1}^{64}y_{i}\geq \sum_{i=1}^{64}1+\sum_{i=1}^{64}x_{i}^{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{64}x_{i}= 48+\sum_{i=1}^{64}( x-\frac{1}{2})^{2}\geq 48$ .
